← Shed install bid calculator

How much to charge to install a shed

Shed dealers get shopped on a published $2,499 installed 10×12 Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the pad or the delivery. A factory-built drop-and-set onto an existing pad with a forklift is a different job from a 12×16 lofted kit with a new gravel pad, a 40-mile crane set, a ramp, extra windows, and old-shed haul-away.

Open the free shed install bid calculator

Price the pad and the delivery, not the 10×12 dump

A backyard shed is a footprint, then a pad, then how it arrives. Length times width is the shed. The pad is that rectangle plus an overhang on every side. An existing pad is a set. New crushed stone is trucks. A new slab is ready-mix. Fifteen forklift miles is not forty crane miles.

Drop-and-set is not a kit

The cheap special is almost always a factory-built unit dropped onto a pad the owner already has. A kit is assembly hours on that pad. Stick-built is lumber and more hours still. Matching a drop-and-set per-foot number on a kit-plus-pad job is how a sold shed becomes a two-day loss after the first gravel ticket.

Ramp, loft, windows, and haul-away are not in the coupon

A ramp is a half-hour and an invoice. Extra windows and a second door are framed openings. A loft is a floor inside the shed. Old-shed haul-away is a dump ticket. The calculator prices the same shed three ways — existing pad, new gravel, new slab — so you can see which pad still keeps the margin when the owner asks you to “just match the other guy.”

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the shed install bid calculator. It is not a structural specification, an engineered stamp, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a shed?

Charge from pad, delivery miles, access, and extras — not a published drop-and-set special. A factory-built 10×12 on an existing pad with a forklift is a different job from a 12×16 lofted kit with a new gravel pad, a crane, a ramp, and old-shed haul-away.

Does the pad change a shed install bid?

Yes. An existing pad is a set. A new crushed-stone pad is trucks and a spread. A new concrete pad is ready-mix and a crew day. Matching an existing-pad special on a kit-plus-pad job is how a sold shed becomes a two-day loss after the first gravel ticket.

How do delivery miles change a shed install price?

Trip hours plus miles, then the delivery invoice. A 15-mile forklift drop is not a 40-mile crane set. The miles do not live in a published 10×12 dump.

Is a kit the same bid as a drop-and-set?

No. Drop-and-set is a unit invoice plus a short set. A kit is assembly hours on the pad. Stick-built is lumber and more hours still. The cheap special is almost always a drop-and-set onto a pad the owner already has.

    Why does “set only” on an existing pad cost so much less than a new gravel or concrete pad?

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Shed Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat installed price per square foot

“$X a square foot installed” is not a price for a shed — it is a price for one specific pad, delivery, access, and scope, quietly applied to every job that calls in.

What a flat installed price per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the shed's footprint by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer or a Facebook special will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — a factory-built drop-and-set onto an existing pad, a short forklift delivery, no ramp, no loft, no haul-away — and then reused for every shed afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the shed's dimensions, fulfillment (factory-built drop-and-set, a kit assembled on site, or stick-built), pad (existing, new crushed-stone, or new concrete), access (forklift or crane), electrical, delivery miles, extra windows and doors, a ramp, a loft, and old-shed haul-away, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the pad, the delivery, the access, and every extra separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat installed price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the shed is a factory-built drop-and-set, a kit assembled on site, or stick-built — even though a stick-built shed alone runs several times the build hours of a drop-and-set of the same footprint. Prices build and set hours and material by fulfillment kit, so drop-and-set, kit, and stick-built are never quoted off the same number.
Has no line for the pad, regardless of whether the shed lands on an existing pad or needs a new crushed-stone or concrete pad poured. Prices pad hours, cubic yards, and material by pad kind — existing, gravel, or slab — so a new pad costs more than a set onto what is already there.
Has no line for delivery miles or crane access, regardless of how far the job is or how tight the site. Prices delivery hours and invoice by the mile, and access hours and equipment separately by forklift or crane, so a 40-mile crane set costs more than a 15-mile forklift drop.
Has no line for a ramp, a loft, extra windows or doors, or old-shed haul-away, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices each extra separately -- ramp, loft, windows, doors, and haul-away -- so a fully loaded job costs more than a bare shell.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two sheds, the same footprint-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($26/hr crew wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $33.89/sq ft rate, applied by footprint aloneGap
10×12 (120 sq ft) factory-built drop-and-set, existing pad, 15 delivery miles, forklift — the job this flat rate was built on$4,066.49 — $33.89/sq ft$4,066.49 (same job, same rate)No gap: this is the one job the flat rate fits.
12×16 (192 sq ft) lofted kit, new gravel pad, 40 delivery miles, crane, ramp, haul-away$8,682.28 bid price; $6,945.82 break-even cost$6,506.39The flat rate quotes $439.44 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $2,175.89 below the calculator's own bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the $33.89/sq ft rate the 10×12 drop-and-set job's own price works out to. Applied to the lofted kit's 192 sq ft, that rate does not just erode margin — it prices below the job's own cost to complete. Run your own shed's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat installed price per square foot get a shed quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is the pad, the delivery, the access, and the extras, not floor area. A 12x16 lofted kit on a new gravel pad, delivered 40 miles with a crane set, a ramp, and old-shed haul-away is doing five jobs a 10x12 factory-built drop-and-set onto an existing pad, delivered 15 miles with a forklift, never touches -- none of which scale with square footage the way a per-square-foot rate assumes. A flat installed rate charges all of that the same as the cheap drop-and-set it was priced from.

What does a flat installed price per square foot usually leave out entirely?

The pad (existing, new gravel, or new concrete), delivery miles, crane versus forklift access, and extras like a ramp, a loft, extra windows or doors, and old-shed haul-away. A job on an existing pad with a short forklift delivery is doing far less than one needing a new gravel pad, a 40-mile crane set, and haul-away -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 10x12 (120 sq ft) factory-built drop-and-set onto an existing pad, 15 delivery miles, forklift access, prices at $4,066.49 -- $33.89 a square foot. Applying that same $33.89 rate to a 12x16 (192 sq ft) lofted kit on a new gravel pad with a 40-mile crane set, a ramp, and old-shed haul-away quotes $6,506.39 -- $439.44 below that job's own $6,945.82 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $2,175.89 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat installed price per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same fulfillment, same pad, similar delivery distance, no crane and no extras either time -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which job it was built on and neither does the estimator until the pad, delivery, access, and extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the shed's dimensions, fulfillment, pad, access, electrical, delivery miles, and extras, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one shed install before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the pad (existing, gravel, or slab), delivery miles, crane versus forklift, drop-and-set versus kit versus stick-built, and a ramp, windows, a loft, and haul-away, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block.
